label: ISS (low Earth orbit)
equipment: ARED (Advanced Resistive Exercise Device) for weight lifting
CEVIS cycle ergometer (shows cycling speed and heart rate)
Ultrasound (used to scan astronauts' muscles in the Sprint study)
gravity: The ISS is weightless. Without Earth's gravity, bone and muscle shrink and weaken, so exercise is critical to keep them healthy.
radiation: The ISS sits just inside Earth's protective magnetic field, but crews still get over ten times the radiation that occurs naturally on Earth.
distance: Communication delay is almost negligible close to Earth. A docked crew vehicle can be a quick ride home, for example in a medical emergency needing surgery.

label: Lunar surface
equipment: No NASA page we opened lists medical equipment for the lunar surface. The items below are for Orion, the spacecraft that carries crews to the Moon.
Six radiation sensors in the Orion cabin (HERA), with on-screen warnings and an audible alarm
Active dosimeters worn by each crew member
A radiation shelter the crew builds from stowage bags in the central part of the crew module
gravity: Surface gravity on the Moon is one-sixth of Earth's. Crews must readjust their balance and coordination after moving between gravity levels.
radiation: The Moon has no protective atmosphere and a weak magnetic field, but the Moon itself blocks some radiation: surface dose is projected near ISS levels, about 0.5 mSv/day.
distance: The Moon is about 238,855 miles (384,400 km) away, roughly a three-day trip. Communication delay close to Earth is almost negligible.
dayLength: The Moon rotates once every 27 Earth days, the same time it takes to orbit Earth.

label: Lunar pressurized rover
equipment: No NASA page we opened lists medical equipment for the pressurized rover.
NASA's habitability study of a five-day rover excursion plans a daily planning conference, a private medical conference, crew exercise and sleep inside the cabin
gravity: Surface gravity on the Moon is one-sixth of Earth's. Crews must readjust their balance and coordination after moving between gravity levels.
radiation: On the lunar surface the Moon itself blocks some radiation: surface dose is projected near ISS levels, about 0.5 mSv/day. The rover cabin is the crew's nearest shelter.
distance: The Moon is about 384,400 km away. Communication delay close to Earth is almost negligible, but the rover is far from any base while it drives.
isolation: The rover carries two astronauts for up to 30 days near the lunar South Pole. NASA's habitability work looks at how the crew lives in the small cabin and at crew fatigue.
dayLength: The Moon rotates once every 27 Earth days, the same time it takes to orbit Earth.

label: Mars transit
equipment: No Mars transit vehicle exists yet, so there is no equipment list to cite.
NASA says a Mars crew must bring all the food, equipment and medical supplies it needs, with no resupply
gravity: Weightless for the whole cruise. Floating can cause dizziness, bone and muscle loss, and vision problems from fluids shifting toward the head.
radiation: Outside Earth's magnetic field, crews face galactic cosmic rays. NASA projects doses of about 1 mSv/day or more beyond low-Earth orbit.
distance: Mars is on average 140 million miles away, and a Mars mission could take roughly three years. One-way messages take about 4 to 24 minutes.
isolation: Crews must handle problems with minimal support from Earth. Sleep loss, body-clock disruption and overwork can add to the strain.

label: Mars surface base
gravity: Crews on Mars will feel about one-third of Earth's gravity, and must readjust after months of weightlessness.
radiation: Mars has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field. Curiosity measured about 210 micrograys per day at the surface, mostly from cosmic rays.
distance: One-way messages take about 4 minutes at closest approach and about 24 minutes at greatest distance, so crews must be self-sufficient.
dayLength: A Mars day (sol) lasts about 24.6 hours, 39 minutes longer than Earth's. Rover teams on Mars time start work 40 minutes later every day.
